name: Cobalamin C deficiency (cblC)
aliases: combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria type cblC
methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria cblC type

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Most common inborn error of intracellular cobalamin (vitamin B12) metabolism, caused by biallelic MMACHC variants
Impaired processing of cobalamin blocks synthesis of both adenosylcobalamin and methylcobalamin, so both dependent pathways fail
Biochemical signature is combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria with low-to-normal methionine
Early-onset (infantile) disease brings failure to thrive, feeding problems, hypotonia, encephalopathy, seizures and a pigmentary retinopathy
Haematological clue is megaloblastic anaemia, sometimes with a thrombotic microangiopathy (haemolytic-uraemic-like picture)
Late-onset disease can present with cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, myelopathy or thromboembolism
Confirmed by plasma/urine metabolites (raised methylmalonic acid and total homocysteine) plus MMACHC sequencing
Treatment centres on parenteral hydroxocobalamin, with betaine, folinic acid and sometimes carnitine; oral B12 is inadequate
reference.pathophysiology: Cobalamin C disease results from deficiency of the MMACHC protein, which performs an early cytosolic step in intracellular processing of dietary cobalamin, dealkylating/decyanating incoming cobalamin so it can be converted into its two active cofactor forms. Loss of function prevents generation of both adenosylcobalamin, the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and methylcobalamin, the cofactor for methionine synthase. Consequently methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be isomerised, causing methylmalonic acid accumulation, and homocysteine cannot be remethylated to methionine, causing hyperhomocysteinaemia with low methionine. The combined metabolic block produces neurological injury, endothelial damage with thrombotic microangiopathy, megaloblastic haematopoiesis and retinopathy. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated methylmalonic acidaemia (mutase or other cobalamin defects)
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy
Other causes of infantile encephalopathy with retinopathy
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film for megaloblastic/haemolytic changes
MMACHC gene sequencing and complementation studies where needed
Renal function and markers of thrombotic microangiopathy
redFlags: Encephalopathy with seizures and rapid neurological deterioration in infancy
Thrombotic microangiopathy with renal impairment (HUS-like presentation)
Severe metabolic acidosis with feeding failure
reference.prognosis: Early-onset disease often has a guarded prognosis with persistent neurological and visual impairment even when treated, whereas late-onset disease responds better to early hydroxocobalamin-based therapy; outcome depends strongly on age at diagnosis and treatment.
pitfalls: Treating with oral cyanocobalamin instead of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, which is far less effective
Diagnosing isolated methylmalonic acidaemia without measuring homocysteine and missing the combined defect
Overlooking the retinopathy, which can progress despite metabolic control
Mistaking the thrombotic microangiopathy for primary atypical HUS
Failing to recognise late-onset presentations with psychiatric or myelopathic features
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Definitive therapy is regular parenteral (intramuscular) hydroxocobalamin to drive residual cofactor synthesis; oral or cyanocobalamin preparations are inadequate
Adjunctive betaine to promote remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, with oral folinic acid and methionine supplementation where methionine is low
Consider L-carnitine to replenish carnitine stores and buffer propionyl-CoA accumulation
Supportive care for neurological and feeding difficulties: seizure control, nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding for failure to thrive, and developmental therapies
Biochemical monitoring of plasma total homocysteine, methylmalonic acid and methionine to titrate treatment
Regular ophthalmological surveillance for pigmentary maculopathy and retinopathy, with vigilance for thrombotic microangiopathy (a haemolytic-uraemic-like picture)
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive MMACHC disorder, with carrier testing and prenatal or newborn-screening options offered to the family
Escalate acute metabolic decompensation during intercurrent illness with intensified hydroxocobalamin, emergency metabolic measures and specialist metabolic-team input
